notes.meaning: Joash became king of Judah while Jehu was ruling the northern kingdom of Israel, and he reigned for forty full years. His mother Zibiah came from Beersheba, a town in the far south of the land. His long rule brought a time of needed stability to the nation after years of wicked leadership and unrest.

Joash obeyed God and ruled well as long as the godly priest Jehoiada was alive to guide him. Jehoiada had protected him as a boy and taught him God's law. Sadly, the king's goodness depended more on his wise teacher than on a deep personal faith of his own. Good mentors are a great blessing, but faith must take root in our own hearts.

Even though Joash followed God, he did not tear down the local hill shrines, called high places. The people were used to offering sacrifices on these hills, even when they meant to worship the true God, instead of going only to the temple in Jerusalem. Leaving these places open allowed bad worship habits to linger in the land.

Joash ordered the priests to gather three types of sacred funds given to the temple. These included the regular census tax required by God's law, money paid to fulfill special promises called vows, and freewill offerings. The king wanted to use all these gifts to restore God's house, which had been badly damaged and neglected.

The king told the priests to collect these funds from the people they knew in their home districts across Judah. They were instructed to use that money directly to fix every broken and decaying part of the temple. Joash remembered how the temple had sheltered him as a child, so he cared deeply about repairing its walls.

More than twenty years into Joash's reign, the priests still had not done the work. They were slow to collect the funds, or they used the gifts for their own living expenses instead of the building. As a result, God's house stayed broken and neglected for years.

Joash called Jehoiada and the other priests to ask why the repairs had not been made. He took the project out of their hands and ordered them to stop collecting money directly from the people. From then on, all funds gathered for the building had to be given over entirely to the repair work.

The priests accepted the king's new plan without complaint. They stepped aside from handling the collection and gave up managing the construction work. This opened the way for a more reliable system that the people could trust.

Jehoiada set up a wooden collection box with a hole drilled through the lid so money could be dropped inside securely. He placed it near the altar, where worshipers entering the temple courtyard could see it. Priests guarding the entrance placed every gift straight into the chest so none of it could be mishandled.

When the chest grew full, the king's royal secretary and the high priest came together to open it. Having both a royal official and a priest present ensured that the counting was honest and open. They weighed the silver and packed it into sealed bags, ready to pay the workers.

The counted silver was handed to trusted managers who oversaw the temple project. These supervisors were regular tradesmen rather than priests, and they used the money to hire carpenters and builders. Putting practical leaders in charge helped the work move forward quickly.

The money paid stonecutters and masons to rebuild damaged walls and buy high-quality timber and cut stone. Every expense needed to make the temple sturdy and beautiful again was covered. Because the money was managed properly, the decaying building was finally restored.

None of this collection was spent on gold or silver items like cups, lamp trimmers, bowls, or trumpets while the construction was underway. The leaders focused every penny on fixing the building itself before making decorative tools for worship. Necessary structural repairs had to come first.

All the money went straight to the craftsmen and laborers who were fixing the building. The temple fabric was restored first so God's house would be secure and honor His name. Once the walls and rooms were finished, other sacred vessels could be provided later.

The king and the high priest did not demand written receipts from the overseers who paid the workmen. These supervisors had proved themselves so completely honest that everyone trusted them. Their faithful character made heavy oversight unnecessary.

Money brought for guilt offerings and sin offerings—sacrifices to make things right after breaking God's law—was kept separate from the repair fund. God's law gave that money directly to the priests for their livelihood. The new repair plan provided for the building without taking away what rightly supported God's ministers.

Later in Joash's reign, King Hazael of Aram invaded the region, captured the city of Gath, and set his sights on Jerusalem. After the priest Jehoiada died, Joash and his leaders had turned away from the Lord to idols. God permitted this dangerous enemy to threaten Judah as a wake-up call and judgment for their unfaithfulness.

Instead of praying and trusting God to defend Jerusalem, Joash stripped the temple and his palace of their gold and sacred gifts. He sent these treasures to Hazael as a bribe so the Aramean army would leave. Buying off the enemy brought only short relief and showed how far the king's faith had fallen.

The rest of Joash's life and reign was recorded in the official royal records of Judah. Other scriptures tell more about how he fell into idolatry and even ordered the murder of Jehoiada's son. His promising start ended in tragedy because he did not stay faithful to God.

Some of Joash's own royal officials plotted against him and murdered him at Beth-millo, a fortified terrace in Jerusalem. They assassinated him in revenge for killing Zechariah, the faithful prophet and son of Jehoiada. Though their violent rebellion was wrong, God allowed it as judgment on Joash's betrayal.

Two of his servants struck Joash down, ending his forty-year reign. He was buried in the City of David, though other scriptures note he was not placed in the honorable tombs of the kings. His son Amaziah then took the throne in his place.
